questions.problem: The maximum  value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum  is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=4:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Therefore,

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$

questions.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=25.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=25:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\ 12 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $12.$ Find a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

 Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

 

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

 This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

 the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

 So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

 we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

 

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 8 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

 Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $||y||=1,$ as usual.

 Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $12,$ we have

 

$$
max\{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1\}={\lambda }_{max}=12.
$$

 Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=12:$

 

$$
\begin{aligned}B-12I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}]-12[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 8 \\ 8 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-12I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

 Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
